passage_title: Temperature, Stirring, and Grain Size in Dissolving Kelsite
passage:
Kelsite is an experimental salt that cools water as it dissolves. Chemists added 5 grams (g) of Kelsite crystals to 200 milliliters of water in a beaker and recorded the time (in seconds, s) until no crystals could be seen, and how much the water's temperature dropped (in °C) while the salt dissolved (see Table 1). Unless stated otherwise, the water started at 30°C, the beaker was stirred at 100 revolutions per minute (rpm), and the crystals were 0.5 millimeters (mm) across.

Experiment 1
The starting water temperature was 10, 20, 30, 40, or 50°C.

Experiment 2
The stirring rate was 0, 50, or 200 rpm. (The result at 100 rpm is that of the 30°C trial in Experiment 1.)

Experiment 3
The crystals were 0.1 mm or 2.0 mm across. (The result for 0.5-mm crystals is that of the 30°C trial in Experiment 1.)
prompt: In Experiment 1, raising the starting water temperature from 40°C to 50°C shortened the time to dissolve by how many seconds?
explanation: Experiment 1: 170 s at 40°C and 160 s at 50°C, a decrease of "10 s".
subskill: compute a difference within a series
topic_tag: Temperature, Stirring, and Grain Size in Dissolving Kelsite
consistency_check: The 30 C / 100 rpm / 0.5 mm trial (205 s, 3.6 C) is listed once and shared by all three experiments; dissolving time levels off above 40 C and above 100 rpm; the salt and its values are invented and follow no named law.

passage_title: Flare Angle, Length, and Wall Material in Torrin Horns
passage:
A Torrin horn is an experimental horn that makes a small speaker sound louder. Engineers fitted the same speaker, playing the same steady tone, into the narrow end of each horn. A meter 2 meters in front of the horn recorded the sound level (in decibels, dB). The engineers also measured the spread: the width (in degrees) of the region in front of the horn where the sound level was within 3 dB of its greatest value (see Table 1). Unless stated otherwise, each horn was made of brass.

Experiment 1
Horns 60 centimeters (cm) long were made with flare angles (how quickly the horn widens) of 5°, 10°, 15°, 20°, or 25°.

Experiment 2
Horns with a 15° flare were made 30, 90, or 120 cm long. (The 60-cm result is that of the 15° horn in Experiment 1.)

Experiment 3
Horns 60 cm long with a 15° flare were made of wood or plastic and compared with the brass horn of Experiment 1.
prompt: In Experiment 1, the loudest sound was produced by the horn with which flare angle?
explanation: Experiment 1 sound levels: 78, 84, 88, 86, and 81 dB for 5° to 25°. The greatest, 88 dB, is at "15°".
subskill: locate a maximum within one series
topic_tag: Flare Angle, Length, and Wall Material in Torrin Horns
consistency_check: The 60 cm / 15 degree brass horn (88 dB, 55 degrees) is listed once and shared by all three experiments; loudness peaks at a 15 degree flare and levels off with length; spread rises steadily with flare; the horn and values are invented, no named law.

passage_title: Depth, Shade, and Fish in Ostry Fen Ponds
passage:
Darter-flies are insects whose young (larvae) live in shallow water and later emerge from the water as winged adults. Ecologists dug ponds in the Ostry Fen, a wetland, and stocked each with the same number of darter-fly eggs. After 6 weeks they counted the larvae per square meter (m²) of pond bottom. At the end of the season they recorded the percent of larvae that emerged as adults (see Table 1). Unless stated otherwise, ponds were unshaded and contained no fish.

Study 1
Ponds were dug 20, 40, 60, 80, or 100 centimeters (cm) deep.

Study 2
Ponds 60 cm deep were covered with netting that shaded 50% or 90% of the water surface. (The unshaded result is that of the 60-cm pond in Study 1.)

Study 3
A pond 60 cm deep was stocked with Kell minnows, small fish native to the fen, and compared with the 60-cm pond of Study 1.
prompt: In Study 1, the pond with the most larvae per m² was how deep?
explanation: Study 1 larvae: 34, 58, 71, 52, and 30 per m² at 20 to 100 cm. The greatest, 71, is at "60 cm".
subskill: locate a maximum within one series
topic_tag: Depth, Shade, and Fish in Ostry Fen Ponds
consistency_check: The 60 cm, unshaded, fish-free pond (71 larvae, 70%) is listed once and shared by all three studies; larvae peak at 60 cm; heavy shade and Kell minnows both cut larvae and emergence; the insect, fish and fen are invented.

passage_title: Why Torvane Solutions Turn Blue
passage:
Torvane is a compound that dissolves in water to make a colorless solution. Stored solutions slowly turn blue. Three scientists explain why.

Scientist 1
Oxygen from the air dissolves into the solution and reacts with torvane to form a blue product. The color forms first at the surface, where the solution touches air, and spreads downward. At 20°C, a solution with air above it shows color within 2 days. A container filled completely and sealed, so that no air is left inside, keeps the solution colorless, whatever the lighting.

Scientist 2
Light breaks torvane apart, and one of the pieces is blue. Because light passes through the whole solution, the color appears evenly throughout rather than starting in one place. Solutions stored in the dark stay colorless, even when open to the air. In direct sunlight, a solution turns blue about twice as fast as in ordinary room light.

Scientist 3
Traces of iron dissolve from metal that touches the solution, such as a steel cap or a steel can, and the iron turns torvane blue. The color forms first next to the metal. The larger the area of metal touching the solution, the faster the color forms. Solutions kept in glass bottles with plastic caps stay colorless, whether or not they are in light or have air above them.
prompt: A completely full, sealed glass bottle with a plastic cap, kept on a sunny windowsill, turns blue. This result is consistent with the view(s) of which scientist(s)?
explanation: Scientist 1 says a full, sealed container stays colorless; Scientist 3 says glass with a plastic cap stays colorless. Only Scientist 2, who blames light, expects the sunlit bottle to turn blue.
domain: Evaluation of Models, Inferences, and Experimental Results
subskill: test viewpoints against a new result
topic_tag: Why Torvane Solutions Turn Blue
consistency_check: Each scientist names a different required condition (air / light / metal contact) and a different place the color starts (surface / evenly / near metal); Scientist 2 alone gives a rate factor (twice as fast in sunlight); each prediction item was checked against all three views.

passage_title: Why Torvane Solutions Turn Blue
passage:
Torvane is a compound that dissolves in water to make a colorless solution. Stored solutions slowly turn blue. Three scientists explain why.

Scientist 1
Oxygen from the air dissolves into the solution and reacts with torvane to form a blue product. The color forms first at the surface, where the solution touches air, and spreads downward. At 20°C, a solution with air above it shows color within 2 days. A container filled completely and sealed, so that no air is left inside, keeps the solution colorless, whatever the lighting.

Scientist 2
Light breaks torvane apart, and one of the pieces is blue. Because light passes through the whole solution, the color appears evenly throughout rather than starting in one place. Solutions stored in the dark stay colorless, even when open to the air. In direct sunlight, a solution turns blue about twice as fast as in ordinary room light.

Scientist 3
Traces of iron dissolve from metal that touches the solution, such as a steel cap or a steel can, and the iron turns torvane blue. The color forms first next to the metal. The larger the area of metal touching the solution, the faster the color forms. Solutions kept in glass bottles with plastic caps stay colorless, whether or not they are in light or have air above them.
prompt: According to Scientist 2, compared with a solution kept in ordinary room light, a solution kept in direct sunlight would turn blue:
explanation: Scientist 2 states that in direct sunlight a solution turns blue "about twice as fast" as in ordinary room light.

passage_title: Why Wedder Frogs Declined in Halley Fen
passage:
Halley Fen is a wetland where Wedder frogs lay their eggs in shallow pools. Surveys counted about 4,800 adult Wedder frogs in the fen in 1990 and about 1,200 in 2020. Three scientists explain the decline.

Scientist 1
In 1994, a drainage ditch was dug along the north edge of the fen, lowering the water table by about 30 centimeters. Tadpoles need a pool to hold water for at least 10 weeks to grow into frogs, and many northern pools now dry out sooner. Frog numbers have fallen since the mid-1990s, and most of the loss has been in the north, near the ditch. Blocking the ditch would let the northern pools recover.

Scientist 2
Since 2001, Tamber reed, a tall plant brought in from elsewhere, has spread across the fen and shades many pools. Tadpoles grow slowly in cool, shaded water, and many die before becoming frogs. The decline began only after the reed spread. Pools that are still free of Tamber reed have as many frogs as they did in 1990.

Scientist 3
A fungus that infects the skin of adult frogs reached the fen in about 1998, probably carried by visiting wading birds. Frog numbers have fallen ever since. Because the fungus spreads through the whole fen, frogs in every part of the fen have declined by about the same proportion.
prompt: Older survey records show that the number of adult frogs was steady from 1990 to 2000 and fell only after 2000. This finding is inconsistent with the view(s) of which scientist(s)?
explanation: Scientist 1 says numbers fell from the mid-1990s and Scientist 3 says they fell from about 1998; both expect a decline before 2000. Scientist 2 says the decline began only after 2001, consistent with the records.
domain: Evaluation of Models, Inferences, and Experimental Results
subskill: test viewpoints against a new result
topic_tag: Why Wedder Frogs Declined in Halley Fen
consistency_check: Each scientist dates the cause differently (1994 ditch / 2001 reed / 1998 fungus) and places the loss differently (north near ditch / reed-covered pools / evenly); 4,800 to 1,200 frogs is a 75% fall; Scientist 1 alone gives the 10-week water requirement.
